title: Comparison at B1
tagline: Say how much bigger, faster or better something is — and use the…the… like a native speaker.
why: B1 Preliminary Speaking Part 2 literally asks you to compare two photos, so modifiers like much, a bit and far are the difference between a flat answer and a natural one. The cloze also loves testing less/the least and as…as, because they're so easy to confuse with the simple -er/-est pattern you learnt at A2.

hook.text: Sofia holds up two jackets. "This one's a bit more expensive, but it's far nicer." Nadia: "True, but that one's not as warm as the blue one." Sofia: "The warmer it is, the happier I am in winter!"
hook.ask: Sofia doesn't just say more expensive — she says a bit more expensive and far nicer. What do a bit and far actually add to the comparison, and what does the warmer… the happier… pattern mean?

items.label: a bit / a little / slightly bigger
far / by far the bigger one

rows.label: Irregular
cells: good→the best, bad→the worst, far→the furthest

rules.rule: one syllable, vowel + consonant: double the consonant
ends in consonant + y: y → i
two or more syllables: use more/most instead

Rule
Example

use.point: Comparatives with modifiers: a bit, much, far, a lot

examples.note: not as + adjective + as = less than

use.point: less, the least, and comparative adverbs

examples.text: This model is less popular than the last one.
That was the least interesting film I've ever seen.
examples.note: the least = opposite of the most

examples.text: Nadia runs more quickly than me, but I swim better.
examples.note: comparative adverbs: more + adverb, or an irregular form like better

watch_out.wrong: This bag is more cheap than that one.
watch_out.right: This bag is cheaper than that one.
watch_out.why: Short adjectives use -er, not more + adjective.
Short adjectives use the -est, not the most + adjective.

watch_out.wrong: She is more good at Maths than me.
watch_out.right: She is better at Maths than me.
watch_out.why: good is irregular: better, not more good.

watch_out.wrong: This jacket isn't so warm than that one.
watch_out.right: This jacket isn't as warm as that one.
watch_out.why: The negative comparison is not as…as, not so…than.

watch_out.wrong: The more you practise, better you get.
watch_out.right: The more you practise, the better you get.
watch_out.why: Both halves of the pattern need the: the…, the….

watch_out.wrong: This is a very more expensive phone.
watch_out.right: This is a much more expensive phone.
watch_out.why: very doesn't modify a comparative — use much, a lot or far instead.

l1.wrong: He is more fast than me.
l1.why: Spanish más + adjective is always more + adjective, but short English adjectives use -er instead.

l1.es: Es el más inteligente de la clase.
l1.wrong: He is the more intelligent of the class.
l1.right: He is the most intelligent in the class.
l1.why: Spanish el más uses el/la + más for everything; English switches between -est and the most, and uses in, not of, with a group.
Spanish drops the second cuanto, but English always repeats the before both comparatives.

l1.es: No es tan alto como su hermano.
l1.wrong: He isn't so tall than his brother.
l1.right: He isn't as tall as his brother.
l1.why: Spanish tan…como becomes as…as in English, never so…than.

remember.trick: Short word, add -ER. Long word, add MORE!
remember.tip: Count the syllables: one (or a short two like happy) → -er/-est. Three or more → more/most. Two is the tricky middle ground, so check the word.

dialogue.title: Choosing a jacket
dialogue.context: Sofia and Nadia are shopping for winter jackets and comparing prices, colours and warmth, while Liam and Mateo wait outside the shop.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: This jacket is a bit more expensive, but it's far nicer than the other one.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: True, but it isn't as warm as the blue one.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: You're right. The warmer it is, the happier I am in winter.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Let's try the cheapest one first, just to compare.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: OK. Actually, this grey one is much better than I expected.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It's also the most comfortable jacket in the shop.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Are you two nearly finished? You're slower than snails!

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Give them time — Sofia always finds the best deal in the end.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Found it! This one is as warm as the expensive one, but much cheaper.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Perfect. The sooner we pay, the sooner we can go and eat.

can_do: I can make comparatives and superlatives, regular and irregular.
I can show how big a difference is with a bit, much, far and slightly.
I can use as…as, not as…as and the…the… to compare things naturally.
summary: Short adjectives take -er/-est; longer adjectives take more/most.
good, bad and far are irregular: better/best, worse/worst, further/furthest.
Modifiers show how big the difference is: a bit/a little/slightly (small) vs much/a lot/far (big).
as + adjective + as = equal; not as + adjective + as = less than.
The + comparative, the + comparative shows two things changing together.
